title: Self-Control in Choices
subtitle: The gap between feeling and acting. And how to use it.
objectives: Define self-control as the gap between feeling and acting
Name the fruit of the Spirit
Use a method in the moment before reacting

cards.title: Self-control is not feeling less
cards.text: It is not calmness and it is not pretending. It is the gap between what you feel and what you do. A gap is a skill, so it can be trained.

cards.title: Where it actually lives
cards.text: Three things happen, and only the middle one is yours.
points: **The feeling arrives.** You did not choose that.
**A gap opens.** This is the part you own.
**An action follows.** Chosen, or not chosen.
**Self-control is what you put in the gap.**

cards.title: The gap between the urge and the move
cards.text: Work it through. Each other choice shows what it would cost.

options: what you do in the gap between feeling and acting
question.explain: The feeling is not the problem. The gap is the work.

cards.title: Two verses that do the work
cards.text: One lists it; the other says what its absence looks like.
points: **Galatians 5:22-23** lists the fruit of the Spirit.
**Self-control is the last of the nine**, not the first.
**Proverbs 25:28:** no self-control is a city with broken walls.
**Not a weak city. An open one.** Anything can walk in.

question.text: Proverbs 25:28 compares a person without self-control to…
options: a city with its walls broken down
question.explain: Not weak. Open. Anything can walk in.

cards.title: Paul uses an athlete on purpose
cards.text: 1 Corinthians 9 is the most literally athletic passage in the letters.
points: **"Every athlete exercises self-control in all things."**
**"I discipline my body."** That is the actual wording.
**Nobody is surprised** that a fighter has rules about food and sleep.
**Same mechanism**, applied to temper.

cards.title: The brakes are still being built
cards.text: This is not an excuse, and it is also a real fact about your age.
points: **The part of the brain that holds the gap** is still developing.
**It keeps developing into your twenties.**
**Which means the gap is shorter now** than it will be.
**And means practising it now** is exactly the right time.

cards.title: The gap, held open
cards.alt: A gloved fist held still a few centimetres from a heavy bag, stopped rather than thrown
cards.text: The feeling arrived. The punch did not. That space is the entire skill.

cards.title: Tilt is the word for losing the gap
cards.text: Every competitive player knows this and most have a rule about it.
points: **You lose, and the next match starts angry.**
**Decisions get worse, so you lose again.**
**The rule is to stop after two.**
**That rule is self-control**, written down in advance.

cards.title: What to remember
points: The feeling is not chosen; the gap is yours.
Galatians 5:22-23 lists self-control last among nine.
Proverbs 25:28. No self-control is a city with no walls.
Notice it, breathe once, ask what you want afterwards.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 1 Devotion. Self-control is defined as a mechanism rather than a mood: the feeling is not chosen, the gap is, and the action follows. That framing matters for this learner specifically, because defining self-control as calmness sets a target he cannot hit, while defining it as the gap gives him something to practise. The interactive walks the gap and answers every other choice with its cost rather than a verdict. The growth lens states the honest fact that the relevant part of the brain is still developing, and turns it into a reason to practise now rather than an excuse. 1 Corinthians 9 carries the boxing lens because the passage is genuinely athletic.
discussion: Ask what self-control is, in his own words.
Ask what Proverbs 25:28 compares it to, and why that image.
Ask what he puts in the gap.
Ask what his own rule after two losses would be.
extension: Have him write his own three-step rule for the gap and put it somewhere visible.
Have him name one moment this week where the gap worked.
misconceptions: "Self-control means not feeling angry." The feeling arrives either way.
"Pretending it is fine counts." It resurfaces elsewhere.
"Proverbs 25:28 says he is weak." It says he is open.
